_comment: All the copy for /how-this-was-built, in reading order. Editable in the browser under `npm run dev`, or in bulk via `npm run copy:export`. The {braced} tokens in facts.*.detail are build-time numbers computed from the files they describe; the page substitutes them. Edit the words around them freely, but keep the braces — a fact with a number typed in would make this page argue against itself. Rewritten 2026-08-06 to show the workflow and link the artefacts. Deliberately the shortest page on the site: it is an easter egg, not a third case study.
title: How this was built
standfirst: A design system where Figma, the code and the build agree, and a build that refuses to ship if they stop.
lead: The first case study argues for one specification that designers, engineers and language models all build from. That project ended before it reached production, so this site is the smallest complete version of the same idea, and rather than a description of the approach it is the approach running, on something you can open.

items.detail: Where the work happens. The repo, the Figma file and the checks are driven from one place, so a change reaches the design file, the code and the tests without a handoff between them.
A live connection into the Figma file. Tokens, components and the layout rules are read and written from the editor rather than exported by hand, which is what stops the file and the repo drifting.
Every push runs the checks below. If Figma and the code disagree, the build stops rather than the disagreement getting noticed later.
Every component rendered inside a band and snapshotted in both themes, so a regression in either one fails the build.

facts.heading: What that adds up to
facts.intro: None of these numbers were typed in. They are computed when this page is built, from the files they describe.

items.detail: {primitives} primitives and {semantic} semantic tokens per theme, exported from Figma and checksum verified against it.
{textStyles}, emitted as CSS custom properties. Type steps between two of them at a breakpoint rather than clamping, so every size on screen exists in the design file.
{components} in code, {specs} with a published contract. The ones with no Figma counterpart have their specs generated from their own TypeScript and stylesheets.
{rules} band adjacency rules, read from the Figma page rather than transcribed. Checksum {checksum}.

{checks} on every push, counted from the gate that runs them rather than from memory. The same gate runs on my machine before the push, so a green run here means the same thing as a green build there. Any one of them failing stops both.

checks.heading: What the build refuses to ship
checks.intro: Each of these exists because something got through without it.
checks._note: Each item is a bold lead-in plus its sentence. Two strings rather than one, because editing is plain text and a <strong> inside a single editable string would be stripped the first time anyone touched it. The CSS item carries a third part because it names a typo that has to set as code.

items.label: Types.
items.text: Nothing else in the repo reads TypeScript. Astro transpiles without checking and Storybook will happily render a story whose props no longer exist, which is how three stale props on Parallax survived the change that removed them.

items.label: Secrets.
items.text: This repo is public, so a committed credential is harvested in minutes and the only cheap moment to catch one is before the push. It scans tracked files only, because the ignored ones legitimately hold the real token, and it never prints what it finds.

items.label: Tokens.
items.text: Every alias resolves, and the export checksum matches the one Figma reproduces from inside the file. A renamed variable fails the build instead of silently rendering nothing.

items.label: Brand packs.
items.text: A brand pack adds its own colours and repoints the same token names the components already use, which is what lets one build serve several brands without a component knowing that brands exist. Every value in a pack has to be an alias rather than a typed colour, both themes have to cover the same tokens, and the checksum has to match the one the brand Figma file produces, so the file and the repository cannot quietly disagree.

items.label: Components.
items.text: Every value in every spec is a token reference. Zero literals, asserted rather than reviewed.

items.label: CSS.
items.text: Every custom property resolves to a real token. A typo like
items.textAfter: is not a CSS error, because it renders as an inherited default and looks deliberate, so nothing else would catch it.

items.label: Contrast.
items.text: Every pairing of text and background the pages actually use, measured for every brand in both themes against the WCAG AA thresholds. See-through colours are composited over whatever sits beneath them first, because a white at seventy per cent is a different colour on every band. Decorative pairs like rules and placeholder outlines are measured and printed rather than failed, since a threshold applied to something it was never meant for gets satisfied by changing a value that was already correct.

items.label: Contracts.
items.text: Every component has a published contract somewhere. The number above says so, and until this check existed that number was right by coincidence rather than by measurement, because two ways of counting happened to cancel.

items.label: Provenance.
items.text: Every image on the site has to say what it is, whether that is a real screenshot, a diagram, a piece of abstract artwork, or a reconstruction that imitates a real interface. Nothing here can check that the answer is honest, because a faked screen is a claim baked into a picture rather than into text, so what this enforces is narrower and still worth having: an image cannot ship until somebody has opened it and written down what they saw.

items.label: Gates.
items.text: The checks that run on a push and the checks that run on this machine have to be the same checks. They were two separate lists for a while and they had already drifted apart, so a clean run here proved nothing about the build, which is the kind of gap that only ever announces itself long after the work has moved on.

items.label: The README.
items.text: The numbers the repository's front page states are checked against the repository. That page is markdown read on GitHub with no build step to substitute into, so unlike this one it cannot compute them; they are typed, and a program asks whether they are still true. It had twice been wrong about how many checks there are, which is a plausible enough sentence that nobody reading it noticed.

items.label: Generated files.
items.text: Regenerating everything has to change nothing. If it does, someone hand-edited a file that is supposed to be measured, and a stale generated file is invisible in a diff because the change you would be looking for is the one that never got made.

items.label: Bands.
items.text: The built pages are linted against the layout rules, and those rules are read from Figma rather than copied. Adding a rule there fails the build here until someone implements it.

items.label: Gaps.
items.text: A missing fact renders on the page as a marker rather than hiding in a comment, so it cannot be quietly forgotten. This reads the built pages and fails if one would ship, which matters most when a new case study is being written and the holes are still being filled.

items.label: Deploy configuration.
items.text: Vercel reads its own config file before it installs anything and before it builds, so a mistake in that one file fails the deployment without ever producing a build log, and every check above stays green while the site quietly keeps serving the build before it. That is how a comment written into it cost eight deployments and a day, found by asking the live site what it was serving rather than by looking at a badge. This reads it: the keys against the ones Vercel accepts, and any rewrite pointing at a path that also exists as a real file, because the file wins and the rule silently never runs.

items.label: The working record.
items.text: CLAUDE.md is the long technical record sitting behind this page, and it states figures that it cannot compute for itself, among them four export checksums. Three of those had sat in it stale while the build was printing something else, each one reading as a perfectly ordinary sentence, so every figure is now read back from the script that prints it rather than trusted where it lies.

limits.heading: What it does not do
paras: It does not check whether the design is any good. It checks that the design and the code are the same thing, which is a narrower claim and the only one worth automating. Taste is still done by looking.

It does not check that the result is usable either. axe-core runs clean across nine pages, two widths and two themes, and the site still shipped a menu that told screen readers it was modal while keyboard focus walked straight out of it, onto a button that was invisible and could not be clicked. No single element was wrong, so nothing automated could see it. A person tabbing through the sheet did.

It only sees what the design file sees. The carousel's back arrow was a right-pointing chevron flipped in CSS, which looked right on screen and left the published contract naming the wrong icon, because a contract is measured from Figma and Figma could not see the flip. Every check passed. What fixed it was drawing the icon.

It stops at the token layer. The contrast check resolves every pairing out of the token files, which is the wrong question for a diagram painted in somebody else's palette. The token-tiers figure resolves a brand's values in CSS as you pick one, with no JavaScript in it at all, so the pair a reader sees exists nowhere but a browser with a theme applied and a selection made. Measured there it was failing in three places, including a label that passed in dark and sat at 3.67:1 in light. What found them was a second script that opens the page and reads the pixels.

links.heading: The receipts
links._note: All three verified open anonymously on 2026-08-07 — Figma by fetching the file thumbnail with no session, Chromatic by reading 54 stories out of index.json, GitHub by cloning with no credentials. Three href rules learned here. The Figma link carries the node-id of the Cover page (56-4384) so it always lands on the cover and the reader picks where to go next, rather than opening wherever the file was last left; the `t=` parameter is stripped because that is a share-session token, not part of the address. The Chromatic link is the branch permalink, not the `library?appId=` URL: the library is the build history and sits behind a login, so it would have read as a closed door to anyone without an account. The permalink is the Storybook itself and needs none. All three open in a new tab, so reading the receipts never costs the reader their place on this page — which is why `newTab` below is appended to each link's accessible name. RE-POINTED 2026-08-19: the Wise and Healf files were replaced, and the two keys recorded until then (`G3HBCm7Dsa6gQ2PKv0Y8g4` and `oC393wMf4jcRjm8qbkWTeG`) now 404 anonymously, so both of those receipts were dead links for a reader while looking perfectly fine in the source. All three files are structural copies of each other and their Cover canvas is `56:4384` in every one, so the node-id is now identical across the three hrefs rather than a per-file value to look up — do not assume that survives a file being rebuilt. Wise uses `node-id=2001-15` and the other two use their Cover canvas id. That is deliberate and supplied twice by Rohit: the Wise cover canvas `56:4384` holds exactly one 1920x1080 frame, `2001:15`, so both ids land on the same artwork and the frame id simply focuses it. Do not normalise it again. Re-verified open anonymously on 2026-08-19 by fetching each file thumbnail with no session, which is the only check that speaks for a reader who has never signed in.
links._figma: THE DEFAULT BRAND HAS NO FIGMA RECEIPT, and that is a deliberate hole rather than an oversight. Every partner block below links its own file, revolut included; this list is the one a stranger on the apex sees, and the only file the shared system lives in is titled "Revolut" in Figma. A URL slug can be written to say anything, but Figma normalises it to the real file name, so the reader would land on a company name on the one hostname deliberately cleared of it. Two receipts that are true beat three where one leaks. NOTE THAT THE FILE IS NOT ORPHANED: revolut.deesyn.com links it, exactly as every other partner hostname links its own. What the apex lacks is a company-neutral file to point at, and restoring it is one object here once such a file exists. The column count follows the list length, so nothing else has to change.
